evidence.title: backend engineering isn’t going away. the “backend engineer” job might. i’m in the camp that AI will create more software jobs, not fewer. but the boundaries of those jobs will ...
evidence.rawVisibleText:
backend engineering isn’t going away. the “backend engineer” job might.

i’m in the camp that AI will create more software jobs, not fewer. but the boundaries of those jobs will change completely. 

specialists still (and probably will for a long time) get the most out of AI. but they’re also expected to work beyond that specialty.

i think roles are converging around two kinds of people:
- builders ship the whole product. they might be strongest in frontend, backend, or infra, but they do whatever is needed to get something into users’ hands.
- researchers work on questions without clear answers. they chase moonshots, test what’s possible, and help decide what should be built next.

specialties won’t disappear. They’ll become an advantage rather than the boundary of the job.

evidence.rawVisibleText:
I think it's interesting that in AI-native organizations, the benchmark when looking at a tool isn't the human who would do the work. 

It's the internal AI tools people have built that are highly-customized to their own work, so the pitch of replacing human doesn't really work because they're already working at 10x of an avg person.

The question then is whether the tool can match the capabilities of internal agents with a few more bells & whistles, but more importantly, whether the tool has checks + guards that make it production-ready across the entire org

Osseus is the secure research brain for R&D teams. Today, research knowledge is fragmented across specialist tools, decisions, messages, and people's minds.

evidence.title: We came in with a product question.
evidence.rawVisibleText:
We came in with a product question. We left with an architecture.

This week, through Y Combinator, we got to sit down with Shai Alon from Google.

Shai has spent years working on search, knowledge graphs, and AI systems, so we used the office hours to go deep on one of the most essential parts of CodeAlmanac: making a codebase wiki truly queryable for agents.

The discussion sharpened how we think about the architecture:
CodeAlmanac is the open-source product we’re building at Almanac (YC S26): a living wiki that gives AI agents queryable context over your codebase.

Instead of an agent only grepping files, it can ask:
> codealmanac search "checkout timeout"

Or find the wiki pages that explain a specific part of the code:
> codealmanac search --mentions src/auth/

Then open the relevant page before making changes:
> codealmanac show auth-flow

Our belief is simple:
better context makes better agents.
If you’re experimenting with agentic development, try CodeAlmanac for free on GitHub:
⭐ https://lnkd.in/gk7zVAG2

Grateful to Shai and YC for office hours that directly shaped the product.

Rohan Sharma Kushagra Chitkara
#YCombinator #Google #GoogleCloud #AgenticDevelopment #DevTools #OpenSource

evidence.rawVisibleText:
OneCLI is backed by Y Combinator (S26) ✅

What a journey...

This was my dream for years, and here we are.

Guy Ben-Aharon and I have been at this a long time. Project after project in the OSS space, learning by shipping. We got ChartDB to 22.5K stars and past $10K MRR, bootstrapping the whole way. No shortcuts, just the two of us and a lot of long nights.

Then AI agents arrived and pulled us back to our first base: 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆. It's where we both come from, and suddenly the thing we knew best was the thing the industry was getting wrong. Everyone was handing agents plaintext credentials and hoping for the best.

So we pivoted to OneCLI. An open source identity gateway for AI agents. It abstracts credentials away and enforces predictable execution through policy-driven rules. The agent does its job, but never holds the keys. You can't steal what isn't there.

We spent years getting ready for a problem we didn't see coming. Now we get to build the answer full time.
Thank you Brad Flora and Christina Gilbert for betting on us. And Guy Ben-Aharon, none of this exists without you.
